caption:
Le Chat, Mistral's AI assistant, is now called Vibe, and your old chats and plan came with it.
Same login at chat.mistral.ai, plus a new Work mode that plans and runs multi-step tasks.
The full guide, with prompts and what the free plan leaves out, is on neurafeedai.com.

Have you tried Mistral's assistant, or do you stick with ChatGPT?

paragraphs.text: If you are looking up how to use Le Chat, the first thing to know is that it has a new name. On May 28, 2026, Mistral AI renamed Le Chat to Vibe, its single assistant for everyday work and for coding. Mistral's help center says your account, plan, conversations and saved content carried over, and you still sign in with the same login at chat.mistral.ai.

Le Chat first launched in February 2024, and iOS and Android apps followed in February 2025. Mistral describes it as a multilingual assistant that can search the web, generate images, write and debug code, summarize documents or simply talk. The help center says it chooses its tools based on what you ask, so you do not have to switch them on for each question.
How to use Le Chat in its new Vibe form

paragraphs.title: 1. Sign in at chat.mistral.ai or in the app
paragraphs.text: Open chat.mistral.ai in a browser, or install the app from the App Store or Google Play. If you had a Le Chat account, use the same login and your old conversations are there. Mistral's help center notes that some features need you to be logged in, so create an account even if you only plan to use the free plan.

paragraphs.title: 2. Choose Chat or Work
paragraphs.text: Vibe has three modes. Chat is the turn by turn conversation Le Chat was known for. Work is for tasks with several steps across your apps and files. Code is for developers. In heise's hands on test, logged in free users switched between Chat and Work with a control in the top left corner of the start screen. Mistral's announcement says Chat mode will be retired, with Le Chat history staying available in Work mode.

paragraphs.title: 3. Write the full task, not a keyword
paragraphs.text: Mistral's help center says the assistant has no prior context about you, so give it specific instructions. Say what you want, what to work from and what the answer should look like. Short keyword queries get generic answers.

paragraphs.title: Prompt 1: A news brief with sources
paragraphs.text: Search the web for news about [topic] from the last 7 days. Give me 5 bullet points, each with one source link. End with one sentence on what to watch next. Leave out anything older than 7 days.

paragraphs.title: 4. Upload a file and ask about it
paragraphs.text: Mistral lists document and image understanding among the core features: you upload a file or picture and ask questions about it. For files you want to reuse, Libraries act as personal knowledge bases you can chat with, and Projects group related chats into folders.

paragraphs.title: Prompt 2: Pull the key facts out of a document
paragraphs.text: Read the attached [contract / report / PDF]. List every date, amount and deadline it mentions in a table with three columns: item, value, page. Then tell me in three sentences what I need to do and by when.

paragraphs.title: 5. Hand a multi-step job to Work mode
paragraphs.text: Work mode is where Vibe differs most from the old Le Chat. According to Mistral, it writes a plan and asks for your approval before it starts, works across connected apps such as Google Workspace, Outlook, SharePoint, Slack and GitHub, and streams its progress. You can expand each tool call to see what went in and what came out. Tasks can also run on a schedule: once, daily, weekly or monthly, with a notification when they finish.

paragraphs.title: Prompt 3: A weekly task for Work mode
paragraphs.text: Every Monday, read the spreadsheet [file name] and compare this week's [sales / signups / expenses] with last week's. Make one chart and a five line summary of what changed, and draft it in a canvas I can send to my team.
Read the plan Work mode shows you before you approve it. It is the cheapest place to catch a wrong file, a wrong inbox or a step you did not ask for.
Features worth knowing

Mistral's capabilities overview lists Think mode, which uses its reasoning model for harder questions; Voice mode, so you can talk instead of type; Deep Research for multi-step web research; a Code Interpreter that runs Python in a secure environment; Canvas, an editor you work in together with the assistant; and image generation with models from Black Forest Labs. The help center adds that web search can draw on news from AFP and AP.

Work mode also has Skills, reusable workflows that Mistral says are built on open standards. In heise's test, skills could be turned on or off one by one, loaded automatically or called by naming them in a prompt, and users could import their own skills written in Markdown. A pre-installed skill-creator helps you build new ones.
Plans and what the free version leaves out

Mistral's announcement lists four plans: Free for quick answers and simple everyday tasks, Pro at $14.99 a month, Team at $24.99 per user a month with a shared workspace and admin controls, and Enterprise with custom deployments. The help center says the free plan includes most features with daily caps, Pro removes the cap on messages, and a discounted Pro plan exists for eligible students and educators.

Exact limits are hard to pin down. heise reported that the free plan cannot create canvases or run remote coding sessions, and that Pro and Team get five times as many web searches and up to 40 times as many image generations as Free, but that Mistral does not publish the underlying numbers. The Decoder also noted that Mistral had not given concrete usage limits for Work mode. heise quoted prices in euros that differ from the dollar prices on Mistral's page, so check the price shown in your own account.
On the free plan, the help center says your conversations may be used to train Mistral's models unless you opt out in your account settings. Do that before you paste in anything private.
Where it falls short

The rename makes Vibe harder to learn than Le Chat was. There are now three modes, one of them due to be retired, and the help pages are split between the old help center and Mistral's developer docs. heise also found rough edges in Work mode: a writing skill could not pull information from connected apps on its own, and pre-installed skills could not be changed with the skill-creator.

The practical approach is to start in Chat with one real question you would otherwise search for, then try Work mode on one small, repeatable job, such as a weekly summary from a single spreadsheet. If the plan it writes matches what you would have done yourself, give it a bigger task. If it keeps hitting the free caps, that is the point to decide whether Pro is worth it for you.
